cards.question_text: What is pretexting in social engineering, and how does it differ from phishing? Give a concrete example of a pretexting attack.
choices: Pretexting is a social engineering technique where the attacker creates a fabricated scenario (the pretext) to obtain information or access. The attacker impersonates a legitimate role — e.g., calling an employee pretending to be IT support who needs their credentials to 'fix a server issue.' Unlike phishing (which casts a wide net via mass emails), pretexting is targeted, relies on a believable story, and often uses phone or in-person contact. The key difference: phishing exploits urgency and fear via email; pretexting exploits authority and trust via a crafted narrative.
Pretexting is the same as phishing — both involve sending fraudulent emails to steal credentials
Pretexting is a technical attack that exploits software vulnerabilities, not a social engineering technique
Pretexting is when an attacker physically follows someone through a secure door without authorization
cards.answer: Pretexting is a social engineering technique where the attacker creates a fabricated scenario (the pretext) to obtain information or access. The attacker impersonates a legitimate role — e.g., calling an employee pretending to be IT support who needs their credentials to 'fix a server issue.' Unlike phishing (which casts a wide net via mass emails), pretexting is targeted, relies on a believable story, and often uses phone or in-person contact. The key difference: phishing exploits urgency and fear via email; pretexting exploits authority and trust via a crafted narrative.
cards.explanation_correct: Pretexting is one of the most effective social engineering vectors because it builds a believable story. Real-world examples: Frank Abagnale impersonated a pilot, doctor, and lawyer. Attackers research their target on LinkedIn/social media to craft a convincing pretext. The pretext establishes authority (I'm from IT/HR/your bank) and urgency (this needs to happen now). Defense: verify identity through a separate channel (call back on a known number), question unusual requests, and train staff to recognize pretexting patterns.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Pretexting is NOT the same as phishing — phishing is email-based and mass-targeted, while pretexting is personalized and narrative-driven. Pretexting is NOT a technical/software attack — it's a human manipulation technique. Pretexting is NOT tailgating (physical following) — it's about creating a false scenario. Common mistakes: (1) not verifying identity through independent channels, (2) assuming phone callers are who they claim to be, (3) sharing information because the caller 'seems to know a lot' (that info came from OSINT), (4) not questioning authority figures, (5) complying with urgent requests without verification.

cards.question_text: Define baiting, tailgating, and shoulder surfing as social engineering attacks. How does each exploit human behavior differently?
choices: Baiting: An attacker leaves a malware-infected device (e.g., USB drive labeled 'Salary Increases 2026') in a location where a target will find and plug it in — exploiting curiosity and greed. Tailgating: An attacker follows an authorized person through a physical security door without authentication — exploiting politeness and social norms (holding the door open). Shoulder surfing: An attacker observes someone's screen or keyboard from nearby to capture passwords, PINs, or sensitive data — exploiting visual exposure in public spaces. Each exploits a different human trait: baiting = curiosity/greed, tailgating = courtesy/social pressure, shoulder surfing = lack of spatial awareness.
Baiting, tailgating, and shoulder surfing are all the same attack — they all involve sending phishing emails
Baiting is when you physically follow someone through a door, tailgating is when you watch their screen, and shoulder surfing is when you leave a USB drive — the names are interchangeable
Baiting is a network scanning technique, tailgating is a man-in-the-middle attack, and shoulder surfing is a password cracking method
cards.answer: Baiting: An attacker leaves a malware-infected device (e.g., USB drive labeled 'Salary Increases 2026') in a location where a target will find and plug it in — exploiting curiosity and greed. Tailgating: An attacker follows an authorized person through a physical security door without authentication — exploiting politeness and social norms (holding the door open). Shoulder surfing: An attacker observes someone's screen or keyboard from nearby to capture passwords, PINs, or sensitive data — exploiting visual exposure in public spaces. Each exploits a different human trait: baiting = curiosity/greed, tailgating = courtesy/social pressure, shoulder surfing = lack of spatial awareness.
cards.explanation_correct: These are physical/social attacks that bypass technical controls entirely. Baiting USB drops were famously tested by researchers who found 60%+ of found USBs were plugged in. The Stuxnet worm initially spread via USB drives. Tailgating is countered by mantraps (dual-door interlock), badge enforcement, and security awareness. Shoulder surfing is countered by privacy screens, positioning monitors away from walkways, and shielding keypads when entering PINs.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: These are NOT the same attack and NOT email-based — they are distinct physical/social techniques. The names are NOT interchangeable — each has a specific meaning. They are NOT technical/network attacks — they exploit human behavior, not software. Common mistakes: (1) confusing baiting with phishing (baiting uses physical devices, phishing uses email), (2) thinking tailgating requires technical skills (it requires social skills), (3) underestimating shoulder surfing in coffee shops/airports, (4) not using privacy screens, (5) holding doors for strangers out of politeness, (6) plugging in found USB drives.

cards.question_text: An employee in your finance department receives an email that appears to be from the CEO, asking them to urgently wire $45,000 to a new vendor for a confidential acquisition. The email says 'Do not discuss this with anyone — it's confidential.' What type of attack is this, and what should the employee do?
choices: This is a Business Email Compromise (BEC) / CEO fraud attack, a targeted form of spear phishing. The red flags are: (1) urgency and confidentiality to prevent verification, (2) unusual financial request bypassing normal procurement流程, (3) sender may be spoofed or the CEO's account may be compromised. The employee should: NOT wire the money, verify the request through a separate channel (call the CEO directly on a known number, not one from the email), report it to the security team, and check email headers for spoofing. BEC attacks caused $2.9 billion in losses globally in 2023 — they are the most financially damaging social engineering attack.
This is a legitimate business request from the CEO — the employee should wire the money immediately since it's marked confidential and urgent
This is a standard phishing email — the employee should just delete it and not report it since no harm was done
This is a ransomware attack — the employee should disconnect their computer from the network and call IT
cards.answer: This is a Business Email Compromise (BEC) / CEO fraud attack, a targeted form of spear phishing. The red flags are: (1) urgency and confidentiality to prevent verification, (2) unusual financial request bypassing normal procurement流程, (3) sender may be spoofed or the CEO's account may be compromised. The employee should: NOT wire the money, verify the request through a separate channel (call the CEO directly on a known number, not one from the email), report it to the security team, and check email headers for spoofing. BEC attacks caused $2.9 billion in losses globally in 2023 — they are the most financially damaging social engineering attack.
cards.explanation_correct: BEC/CEO fraud is the costliest cybercrime per the FBI IC3 report. Key indicators: authority (CEO/CFO impersonation), urgency (act now), secrecy (don't tell anyone), and financial anomaly (bypasses normal流程). Defense: out-of-band verification (ALWAYS verify financial requests by phone/in-person), dual authorization for wire transfers, email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), and training finance staff specifically on BEC. The 'don't discuss this' instruction is a deliberate tactic to prevent the target from checking with colleagues.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: This is NOT a legitimate request — the urgency + secrecy combination is a classic BEC red flag. It is NOT a standard phishing email to just delete — BEC must be reported because the CEO's account may be compromised and other employees may receive similar requests. It is NOT ransomware — no encryption is involved. Common mistakes: (1) complying with urgent financial requests without verification, (2) not using out-of-band verification, (3) trusting the displayed sender name (check the actual email address), (4) not having dual-authorization for wire transfers, (5) not reporting BEC attempts, (6) not implementing DMARC to detect email spoofing.

cards.question_text: During a penetration test, the tester calls the help desk pretending to be a new employee who locked themselves out of their account. They provide the employee's name, department, and manager's name (all found on LinkedIn), and ask for a password reset. The help desk complies. What principle was violated, and what controls should prevent this?
choices: The principle violated is identity verification — the help desk reset the password without properly verifying the caller's identity. The attacker used OSINT (LinkedIn) to build credibility but was never authenticated. Controls that should prevent this: (1) Mandatory identity verification before any password reset — using pre-registered challenge questions, callback to a known phone number, or manager approval. (2) Help desk procedures that require a ticket number from the user's manager for new employee lockouts. (3) Awareness training for help desk staff on social engineering. (4) Password resets should require multi-factor verification (e.g., send a code to the registered MFA device). (5) Log all password reset requests for audit.
The help desk did nothing wrong — they were just being helpful to a new employee who was locked out
The principle violated was network security — the attacker should not have been able to call the help desk phone number
The problem is that the employee's information was on LinkedIn — LinkedIn should be banned for all employees
cards.answer: The principle violated is identity verification — the help desk reset the password without properly verifying the caller's identity. The attacker used OSINT (LinkedIn) to build credibility but was never authenticated. Controls that should prevent this: (1) Mandatory identity verification before any password reset — using pre-registered challenge questions, callback to a known phone number, or manager approval. (2) Help desk procedures that require a ticket number from the user's manager for new employee lockouts. (3) Awareness training for help desk staff on social engineering. (4) Password resets should require multi-factor verification (e.g., send a code to the registered MFA device). (5) Log all password reset requests for audit.
cards.explanation_correct: Help desks are prime targets for social engineering because they're trained to be helpful. The attacker exploits the 'helpfulness bias' — the desire to assist. The fact that the caller knows the employee's name, department, and manager is NOT verification — that information is publicly available. Proper verification requires something the caller knows that ISN'T public (pre-registered challenge response) or something they have (registered MFA device). This is why callback verification is critical — you call the number ON FILE, not a number the caller provides.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: The help desk absolutely did something wrong — resetting a password without identity verification is a security failure. The problem is NOT network security — it's a procedural/human failure. Banning LinkedIn is impractical and doesn't solve the core issue — verification procedures must work regardless of what information is public. Common mistakes: (1) treating public information as identity proof, (2) not requiring callback verification, (3) not having formal password reset procedures, (4) help desk staff not trained on social engineering, (5) no MFA on the reset process, (6) no audit logging of resets.

cards.question_text: Your organization has experienced three social engineering incidents in 6 months: (1) A finance employee wired $80K to a BEC attacker, (2) The help desk reset 3 passwords for an attacker impersonating employees, (3) A manager clicked a malicious link in a spear-phishing email that led to credential theft. Design a comprehensive anti-social-engineering program covering technical controls, policies, and training. How would you measure its effectiveness?
choices: Comprehensive anti-social-engineering program: TECHNICAL: (1) Email security — SPF, DKIM, DMARC (reject policy), email filtering with AI-based BEC detection, banner warnings on external emails. (2) MFA everywhere — phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn) for sensitive accounts, NOT SMS-based. (3) Password reset process — callback verification to registered numbers, manager approval workflow, MFA challenge before reset. (4) Endpoint protection — EDR to detect credential theft and malicious payloads. POLICIES: (1) Financial verification policy — all wire transfers >$10K require dual authorization and out-of-band verification (call back on known number). (2) Help desk verification SOP — mandatory identity verification steps, ticket-based reset workflow. (3) Acceptable use policy — prohibit plugging in found USB drives. TRAINING: (1) Role-specific training — finance staff get BEC training, help desk gets vishing training, executives get spear-phishing training. (2) Regular phishing simulations (monthly) with immediate feedback. (3) Reporting culture — easy one-click 'Report Phishing' button, no punishment for reporting, positive reinforcement. MEASUREMENT: (1) Phishing simulation click rate over time (target: <5%), (2) Report rate (percentage of simulated phishing that gets reported — target: >40%), (3) Time to report (median time between email arrival and report), (4) Number of actual incidents per quarter, (5) Help desk verification compliance audits, (6) Financial verification compliance audits. Continuous improvement: quarterly review of simulation results, adjust training based on weak areas, track industry benchmarks.
Just install better antivirus software and send an annual security awareness email to all employees — that's sufficient to stop social engineering
Ban all external emails and phone calls — if employees can't receive communications from outside, social engineering can't happen
Fire the employees who fell for the attacks and hire new ones — the problem is individual incompetence, not systemic gaps
cards.answer: Comprehensive anti-social-engineering program: TECHNICAL: (1) Email security — SPF, DKIM, DMARC (reject policy), email filtering with AI-based BEC detection, banner warnings on external emails. (2) MFA everywhere — phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn) for sensitive accounts, NOT SMS-based. (3) Password reset process — callback verification to registered numbers, manager approval workflow, MFA challenge before reset. (4) Endpoint protection — EDR to detect credential theft and malicious payloads. POLICIES: (1) Financial verification policy — all wire transfers >$10K require dual authorization and out-of-band verification (call back on known number). (2) Help desk verification SOP — mandatory identity verification steps, ticket-based reset workflow. (3) Acceptable use policy — prohibit plugging in found USB drives. TRAINING: (1) Role-specific training — finance staff get BEC training, help desk gets vishing training, executives get spear-phishing training. (2) Regular phishing simulations (monthly) with immediate feedback. (3) Reporting culture — easy one-click 'Report Phishing' button, no punishment for reporting, positive reinforcement. MEASUREMENT: (1) Phishing simulation click rate over time (target: <5%), (2) Report rate (percentage of simulated phishing that gets reported — target: >40%), (3) Time to report (median time between email arrival and report), (4) Number of actual incidents per quarter, (5) Help desk verification compliance audits, (6) Financial verification compliance audits. Continuous improvement: quarterly review of simulation results, adjust training based on weak areas, track industry benchmarks.
cards.explanation_correct: Social engineering defense requires defense-in-depth because no single control is sufficient. The program addresses all three incidents: BEC (financial verification policy + email security), help desk vishing (verification SOP + callback), spear phishing (FIDO2 MFA + training + reporting). The key insight: social engineering exploits humans, so the program must combine technical controls (make the attack harder), policies (define expected behavior), and training (build recognition skills). Measurement is critical — click rate alone is misleading; you need report rate (are people recognizing AND reporting?) and time-to-report (how fast do they react?). A healthy security culture reports more and clicks less.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Antivirus alone is useless against social engineering — the attack targets the human, not the software. Banning external communication is not feasible for a business. Firing employees who fall for attacks creates a culture of fear where people hide incidents instead of reporting them — the opposite of what you want. Common mistakes: (1) treating security awareness as a one-time annual training (it must be continuous and simulated), (2) using punishment instead of positive reinforcement, (3) not tailoring training to role-specific risks, (4) not measuring effectiveness, (5) relying only on technical controls without addressing human behavior, (6) not having a simple reporting mechanism, (7) not implementing phishing-resistant MFA (SMS MFA can be bypassed via SIM swapping).

cards.question_text: What is the difference between vulnerability scanning and penetration testing? When should each be used, and what are their limitations?
choices: Vulnerability scanning is an automated process that identifies known vulnerabilities (CVEs, misconfigurations, missing patches) across systems using a scanner (Nessus, Qualys, OpenVAS). It's broad, fast, repeatable, and should be run regularly (weekly/monthly). Limitations: produces false positives, doesn't exploit vulnerabilities, doesn't assess business impact. Penetration testing is a manual, targeted process where a tester actively exploits vulnerabilities to determine real-world impact and access. It's deep, slow, expensive, and done periodically (annually or before major releases). Limitations: point-in-time snapshot, limited scope, depends on tester skill. Use scanning for continuous visibility; use pentesting for validation and depth.
Vulnerability scanning and penetration testing are the same thing — both involve automatically scanning systems for vulnerabilities
Penetration testing is automated and fast, while vulnerability scanning is manual and slow — the names are reversed
Vulnerability scanning finds malware, while penetration testing removes it — they are both types of antivirus
cards.answer: Vulnerability scanning is an automated process that identifies known vulnerabilities (CVEs, misconfigurations, missing patches) across systems using a scanner (Nessus, Qualys, OpenVAS). It's broad, fast, repeatable, and should be run regularly (weekly/monthly). Limitations: produces false positives, doesn't exploit vulnerabilities, doesn't assess business impact. Penetration testing is a manual, targeted process where a tester actively exploits vulnerabilities to determine real-world impact and access. It's deep, slow, expensive, and done periodically (annually or before major releases). Limitations: point-in-time snapshot, limited scope, depends on tester skill. Use scanning for continuous visibility; use pentesting for validation and depth.
cards.explanation_correct: Scanning and pentesting are complementary, not interchangeable. Scanning provides breadth (find all CVEs across 1000s of systems) but not depth (is this exploitable?). Pentesting provides depth (chain exploits, pivot, demonstrate impact) but not breadth (limited scope). Best practice: scan continuously, pentest annually or after major changes. A vulnerability scanner finding 500 CVEs doesn't tell you which 5 are actually exploitable in your environment — that's what pentesting validates. Compliance frameworks (PCI DSS) require both.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: They are NOT the same — scanning is automated identification, pentesting is manual exploitation. The names are NOT reversed — scanning IS automated and fast, pentesting IS manual and slow. Neither finds or removes malware — that's antivirus/EDR. Common mistakes: (1) relying only on scanning without pentesting (false sense of security), (2) relying only on pentesting without scanning (gaps between tests), (3) not remediating scan findings because 'pentesting didn't find it exploitable,' (4) treating scanner output as ground truth (false positives exist), (5) not credentialed scanning (missing internal vulnerabilities), (6) pentesting with too narrow a scope.

cards.question_text: What is CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) and how does it relate to CVSS? Explain how security teams use these two systems together.
choices: CVE is a standardized identifier system for publicly known cybersecurity vulnerabilities — each vulnerability gets a unique CVE ID (e.g., CVE-2024-12345) that provides a reference number for tracking. CVE is maintained by MITRE and provides a description but not a severity rating. CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) is a scoring framework (0.0-10.0) that rates the severity of a CVE based on exploitability and impact metrics. CVSS v3.1 has Base (inherent), Temporal (changes over time), and Environmental (context-specific) score groups. Security teams use them together: CVE identifies WHAT the vulnerability is (naming/lookup), CVSS tells you HOW BAD it is (prioritization). A CVE without a CVSS score is just an identifier; a CVSS score without a CVE lacks context.
CVE and CVSS are the same system — both are vulnerability scoring systems that assign a number from 1 to 10
CVE is a scoring system and CVSS is an identification system — the descriptions are reversed
CVE is a commercial product sold by vendors, and CVSS is a free alternative — they are competing products
cards.answer: CVE is a standardized identifier system for publicly known cybersecurity vulnerabilities — each vulnerability gets a unique CVE ID (e.g., CVE-2024-12345) that provides a reference number for tracking. CVE is maintained by MITRE and provides a description but not a severity rating. CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) is a scoring framework (0.0-10.0) that rates the severity of a CVE based on exploitability and impact metrics. CVSS v3.1 has Base (inherent), Temporal (changes over time), and Environmental (context-specific) score groups. Security teams use them together: CVE identifies WHAT the vulnerability is (naming/lookup), CVSS tells you HOW BAD it is (prioritization). A CVE without a CVSS score is just an identifier; a CVSS score without a CVE lacks context.
cards.explanation_correct: CVE provides the common language — when someone says 'CVE-2024-12345' everyone knows exactly which vulnerability they mean, regardless of vendor. CVSS provides the prioritization — 'this CVE has a Base score of 9.8 (Critical)' tells you to patch it first. The Environmental score is crucial: a Critical CVE on an internet-facing server is urgent; the same CVE on an isolated test server is lower priority. This is why vulnerability management platforms calculate Environmental scores based on your asset context. NVD (National Vulnerability Database) maps CVEs to CVSS scores.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: CVE and CVSS are NOT the same — CVE is identification (naming), CVSS is scoring (severity). The descriptions are NOT reversed. Neither is a commercial product — both are free, open standards. Common mistakes: (1) treating CVSS Base score as the only priority factor (ignoring Environmental context), (2) not knowing the difference between Base, Temporal, and Environmental scores, (3) trying to patch ALL CVEs equally (impossible — prioritize by CVSS + asset criticality), (4) not tracking CVEs that affect your specific software stack, (5) ignoring CVEs with public exploits (even if CVSS is moderate, exploit availability increases risk).

cards.question_text: A vulnerability scan of your network reveals 1,200 vulnerabilities: 20 Critical (CVSS 9+), 150 High (7-8.9), 400 Medium (4-6.9), and 630 Low (0-3.9). You have a team of 3 sysadmins who can remediate approximately 30 vulnerabilities per week. How should you prioritize and what remediation strategy should you use?
choices: Prioritization strategy: (1) Start with the 20 Critical vulnerabilities — especially those on internet-facing systems with known public exploits. Patch these within 48-72 hours. (2) Then address High vulnerabilities on critical assets (production servers, domain controllers, databases) — target 2 weeks. (3) Use risk-based prioritization: factor in asset criticality, exposure (internet-facing vs internal), and exploit availability (CISA KEV catalog) — not just CVSS alone. (4) For Medium/Low: schedule during regular maintenance windows, use automated patching where possible. (5) Accept risk for Low vulnerabilities on non-critical systems with documented risk acceptance. (6) Implement compensating controls (WAF rules, network segmentation) for vulnerabilities that can't be patched immediately. (7) Re-scan after remediation to verify fixes. The team should focus on risk reduction, not just vulnerability count reduction.
Patch all 1,200 vulnerabilities starting from the lowest CVSS score and working up — this way you clear the most vulnerabilities fastest
Ignore the scan results — 1,200 vulnerabilities is normal and most won't be exploited. Wait until something breaks
Only patch the 20 Critical ones and ignore everything else — if it's not Critical, it's not important
cards.answer: Prioritization strategy: (1) Start with the 20 Critical vulnerabilities — especially those on internet-facing systems with known public exploits. Patch these within 48-72 hours. (2) Then address High vulnerabilities on critical assets (production servers, domain controllers, databases) — target 2 weeks. (3) Use risk-based prioritization: factor in asset criticality, exposure (internet-facing vs internal), and exploit availability (CISA KEV catalog) — not just CVSS alone. (4) For Medium/Low: schedule during regular maintenance windows, use automated patching where possible. (5) Accept risk for Low vulnerabilities on non-critical systems with documented risk acceptance. (6) Implement compensating controls (WAF rules, network segmentation) for vulnerabilities that can't be patched immediately. (7) Re-scan after remediation to verify fixes. The team should focus on risk reduction, not just vulnerability count reduction.
cards.explanation_correct: Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Asset Value. A Critical CVE on an internet-facing web server with a public exploit is a ticking bomb. The same CVE on an isolated backup server is lower risk. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog is invaluable — if a CVE is on the KEV list, it IS being exploited in the wild, bump it to the top. At 30/week, it takes 40 weeks to clear everything — so prioritization is essential. Compensating controls (virtual patching via WAF/IPS) buy time when immediate patching isn't possible (e.g., legacy systems that break with patches).
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Starting from lowest CVSS is backwards — you fix the highest risk first. Ignoring scan results is negligent — known vulnerabilities are the easiest attack path. Only fixing Critical and ignoring High/Medium is short-sighted — attackers chain Medium vulns to gain access, then escalate. Common mistakes: (1) prioritizing by CVSS alone without asset context, (2) not checking for public exploits/KEV catalog, (3) not using compensating controls for unpatchable systems, (4) not re-scanning to verify remediation, (5) not documenting risk acceptance, (6) not automating patching where possible, (7) treating vulnerability management as a one-time project instead of a continuous process.

cards.question_text: Your organization runs a legacy application that is critical for operations but has a known SQL injection vulnerability (CVE with CVSS 9.8). The vendor went out of business and there is no patch available. The application cannot be replaced for 18 months. What compensating controls should you implement, and what is the risk management process?
choices: Compensating controls: (1) Web Application Firewall (WAF) — deploy rules to detect and block SQL injection patterns (virtual patching) — this is the primary compensating control. (2) Network segmentation — isolate the legacy application in its own VLAN/subnet with strict firewall rules limiting access to only necessary systems. (3) Input validation proxy — place a reverse proxy in front that sanitizes input before it reaches the application. (4) Database controls — use a read-only database account for the application where possible, implement least-privilege DB permissions, and enable database activity monitoring. (5) Enhanced monitoring — deploy IDS/IPS signatures for SQLi, monitor database queries for anomalies, alert on suspicious patterns. (6) Access controls — restrict who can access the application (IP allowlisting, VPN-only access, MFA). Risk management process: (1) Document the risk in the risk register with full details (CVE, impact, likelihood, existing controls). (2) Perform a formal risk assessment and get executive sign-off on risk acceptance. (3) Set a remediation deadline (18-month replacement). (4) Review quarterly — verify compensating controls are effective. (5) Have an incident response plan specific to this vulnerability.
Shut down the legacy application immediately — no application is worth running with a CVSS 9.8 vulnerability, regardless of business impact
Just accept the risk and do nothing — since there's no patch, there's nothing you can do
Wait for a new vendor to buy the old company and release a patch — someone will eventually fix it
cards.answer: Compensating controls: (1) Web Application Firewall (WAF) — deploy rules to detect and block SQL injection patterns (virtual patching) — this is the primary compensating control. (2) Network segmentation — isolate the legacy application in its own VLAN/subnet with strict firewall rules limiting access to only necessary systems. (3) Input validation proxy — place a reverse proxy in front that sanitizes input before it reaches the application. (4) Database controls — use a read-only database account for the application where possible, implement least-privilege DB permissions, and enable database activity monitoring. (5) Enhanced monitoring — deploy IDS/IPS signatures for SQLi, monitor database queries for anomalies, alert on suspicious patterns. (6) Access controls — restrict who can access the application (IP allowlisting, VPN-only access, MFA). Risk management process: (1) Document the risk in the risk register with full details (CVE, impact, likelihood, existing controls). (2) Perform a formal risk assessment and get executive sign-off on risk acceptance. (3) Set a remediation deadline (18-month replacement). (4) Review quarterly — verify compensating controls are effective. (5) Have an incident response plan specific to this vulnerability.
cards.explanation_correct: When patching is impossible, compensating controls reduce residual risk to acceptable levels. Virtual patching via WAF is industry standard — ModSecurity, Cloudflare, AWS WAF can block SQLi patterns even when the app itself is vulnerable. Network segmentation limits blast radius — if the app is compromised, the attacker can't pivot. This is a textbook risk acceptance scenario: the business accepts the residual risk (after compensating controls) because the operational impact of shutting down is greater than the security risk. The key is that risk acceptance must be documented, time-limited, and reviewed — not just 'we'll deal with it later.'
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Shutting down the application ignores business impact — risk management balances security and operations. Doing nothing is negligent — compensating controls exist precisely for this scenario. Waiting for a vendor that doesn't exist is not a plan. Common mistakes: (1) not implementing WAF/virtual patching, (2) not segmenting the legacy system, (3) not documenting risk acceptance formally, (4) not reviewing compensating controls periodically, (5) not having an IR plan for when (not if) it's exploited, (6) not using least-privilege DB accounts, (7) treating 'no patch available' as 'nothing can be done.'

cards.question_text: You are building a vulnerability management program from scratch for a 500-employee SaaS company with hybrid infrastructure (AWS cloud + on-prem data center, 200 EC2 instances, 50 on-prem servers, 300 endpoints, 50 containers, and 20 third-party SaaS apps). Design the complete program: tooling, scanning cadence, prioritization framework, remediation SLAs, metrics, and governance. How would you handle cloud-native and container vulnerabilities differently from traditional infrastructure?
choices: VULNERABILITY MANAGEMENT PROGRAM: TOOLING: (1) Network/endpoint scanner — Nessus or Qualys for EC2, on-prem servers, and endpoints (credentialed scans). (2) Container scanning — Trivy or Snyk integrated into CI/CD pipeline (scan images at build time) and registry (scan on push). (3) Cloud configuration scanning — AWS Security Hub + CIS Benchmarks via AWS Config. (4) IaC scanning — tfsec/Checkov on Terraform templates in CI/CD. (5) SaaS posture — SSPM tool for third-party SaaS config (e.g., Microsoft 365, Salesforce). (6) Vulnerability intelligence — integrate CISA KEV, ExploitDB, vendor advisories. SCANNING CADENCE: (1) EC2/on-prem servers — weekly credentialed scans. (2) Endpoints — daily via agent. (3) Containers — every build + daily registry scan. (4) Cloud config — continuous (event-driven). (5) External attack surface — monthly. PRIORITIZATION FRAMEWORK: Risk score = CVSS Base × Asset Criticality × Exposure Factor × Exploit Availability (KEV/ExploitDB). Tier 1: Critical assets (production DBs, auth servers) — any vuln ≥7.0 is high priority. Tier 2: Internal servers — vulns ≥9.0. Tier 3: Dev/test — vulns ≥9.0 with exploits. REMEDIATION SLAs: Critical (CVSS 9+ on Tier 1): 48 hours. High (7-8.9 on Tier 1): 7 days. Critical on Tier 2/3: 14 days. Medium: 30 days. Low: 90 days or risk accept. METRICS: (1) Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) by severity. (2) Vulnerability density (vulns per 100 assets). (3) % of Critical vulns remediated within SLA. (4) Scan coverage (% of assets scanned). cards.question_text: What is a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) system? Describe its core functions, common data sources, and the difference between rules-based detection and behavioral/anomaly-based detection.
choices: A SIEM is a security platform that aggregates, correlates, and analyzes log data from across the organization to detect threats, investigate incidents, and support compliance. Core functions: (1) Log collection — ingests data from firewalls, IDS/IPS, endpoints, servers, cloud services, applications. (2) Normalization — converts disparate log formats into a common schema. (3) Correlation — combines events across sources/time to identify attack patterns (e.g., failed logins + successful login + data exfil = potential compromise). (4) Alerting — generates alerts when correlation rules trigger. (5) Dashboards/reporting — visualizes security posture and compliance. (6) Threat intelligence integration — enriches events with IOCs. Rules-based detection: predefined rules/correlation logic (if X and Y happen within Z minutes, alert) — high precision, low false positives, but misses novel attacks. Behavioral/anomaly detection: uses baselines and ML to flag deviations from normal — catches unknown attacks, but higher false positive rate and requires tuning.

A SIEM is a firewall that blocks network traffic based on port and protocol rules

cards.question_text: What is the difference between IDS (Intrusion Detection System) and IPS (Intrusion Prevention System)? Explain the deployment modes (inline vs passive) and the trade-offs of each.
choices: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) is a passive monitoring system that inspects network traffic and alerts on suspicious activity but does NOT block it — it's deployed out-of-band (connected to a SPAN/mirror port or network tap). IDS has zero impact on network performance and won't accidentally block legitimate traffic, but it can't stop an attack in progress. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) is an active system deployed inline (traffic passes through it) that can drop malicious packets, reset connections, or block IPs in real-time. IPS stops attacks but can introduce latency, cause false positive blocks (disrupting legitimate traffic), and becomes a single point of failure if it goes down. Trade-off: IDS = visibility without disruption (monitoring); IPS = active defense with risk of disruption (prevention). Many organizations use IDS for monitoring/visibility and IPS at perimeter for blocking. Modern NGFWs (Next-Gen Firewalls) often include IPS functionality inline.
IDS and IPS are identical — both block malicious traffic in real-time, the only difference is the name
IDS blocks traffic and IPS only monitors — the descriptions are reversed from what they actually do
IDS is for wireless networks and IPS is for wired networks — they detect different types of attacks based on network type

cards.question_text: Your SOC receives 5,000 alerts per day from the SIEM. You have 5 analysts who can investigate approximately 50 alerts per day (10 each). The majority of alerts are false positives. What strategies should you implement to address this alert fatigue and improve SOC effectiveness?
choices: Strategies to combat alert fatigue: (1) Alert tuning and correlation rule optimization — analyze false positive patterns and adjust thresholds, add contextual filters (e.g., suppress alerts for known scanning from vulnerability scanners). (2) Alert triage/prioritization — implement risk scoring that ranks alerts by asset criticality, threat intel correlation, and severity — analysts focus on top-priority alerts first. (3) SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) — automate repetitive investigation steps: auto-enrich alerts with threat intel, auto-close low-risk alerts that match known-benign patterns, auto-isolate compromised endpoints. (4) UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics) — reduce noise by focusing on anomalous behavior rather than every rule match. (5) Alert suppression/aggregation — group related alerts (e.g., 100 failed logins from one IP = one incident, not 100 alerts). (6) Metrics-driven improvement — track false positive rate per rule, time-to-triage, and analyst feedback to continuously refine rules. (7) Staffing — calculate needed analyst capacity and justify headcount or outsource tier-1 triage to an MSSP. Target: reduce actionable alert volume to match analyst capacity while ensuring no critical alerts are missed.
Just delete all low-priority alerts and only look at Critical ones — if analysts can't handle the volume, reduce it by ignoring most alerts
Fire half the analysts and hire one expensive expert who can handle everything — quality over quantity
Turn off the SIEM — if it's generating too many alerts, it's not working properly and should be disabled

cards.question_text: A security analyst notices that a user account is accessing files outside their normal pattern — downloading large amounts of customer data from a SharePoint site at 2 AM from an IP in a different country. choices: Investigation steps: (1) IMMEDIATE CONTAINMENT — disable the user account and revoke active sessions to stop potential data exfiltration. (2) MITRE ATT&CK mapping: Tactic: Collection (TA0009) — gathering customer data; Technique: Data from Information Repositories (T1213) — SharePoint access; Tactic: Exfiltration (TA0010) — downloading large amounts; Technique: Exfiltration over Web Service (T1567) if data goes to cloud storage. The anomalous access also suggests Initial Access via compromised credentials (T1078). (3) INVESTIGATION — check authentication logs: was MFA bypassed? Was there a SIM swap? Check session tokens — were they stolen? Review all file access/download logs for this session. (4) SCOPE — check if other accounts show similar patterns (broader campaign). (5) EVIDENCE — preserve logs, session data, IP geolocation, user agent strings. (6) IMPACT ASSESSMENT — what data was accessed/downloaded? Is it regulated (PII, PHI)? Breach notification obligations? (7) REMEDIATION — reset credentials, revoke all tokens, force MFA re-enrollment, block the foreign IP, review SharePoint access policies. (8) DOCUMENT — full incident timeline for post-incident review.

cards.question_text: Design a security monitoring architecture for a cloud-native company (100% AWS, 50 microservices, 200 EC2 instances, RDS databases, S3 data lakes, API Gateway, CloudFront). The company has 5-person SOC operating 24/7 in follow-the-sun model. choices: SECURITY MONITORING ARCHITECTURE: LOG SOURCES: (1) AWS CloudTrail — all API calls (management + data events). (2) VPC Flow Logs — network traffic. (3) CloudWatch Logs — application logs from microservices. (4) GuardDuty — threat detection (malicious IP, unauthorized access, crypto-mining). (5) AWS Config — configuration changes and compliance. (6) S3 access logs — data access patterns. (7) RDS audit logs — database queries. (8) ALB/CloudFront access logs — web traffic. (9) EDR on EC2 — endpoint telemetry. (10) API Gateway logs — API access. DETECTION STRATEGY: Layer 1 (AWS-native): GuardDuty for automated threat detection, Security Hub for aggregated findings, Config Rules for compliance. Layer 2 (SIEM): Centralize all logs in Splunk/Sentinel (via Kinesis Firehose) for correlation — cross-source rules (e.g., CloudTrail API call + VPC flow + S3 access = data exfiltration detection). Layer 3 (UEBA): baseline user/service behavior, alert on anomalies (e.g., service account accessing S3 buckets it never accessed before). Layer 4 (Threat Intel): enrich with CISA KEV, AbuseIPDB, commercial feeds. Auto-response: isolate compromised EC2 via Systems Manager, revoke IAM tokens, block IPs in WAF. THREAT HUNTING: (1) Hypothesis-driven: 'Are any IAM roles being used from unexpected regions?' Query CloudTrail. (2) IOC-driven: search for known-bad IPs/hashes across all log sources. (3) TTP-driven: use MITRE ATT&CK to hunt for specific techniques (e.g., T1078 valid accounts from new locations). Schedule weekly hunts, document findings, create new detections from hunt results. (7) Dwell time (time attacker is in environment before detection). (8) Hunt findings per month. (9) Auto-response rate (% of alerts handled by SOAR without human). Target: MTTD < 1 hour, MTTR < 4 hours, >70% auto-response for low-severity alerts.

cards.question_text: What is data classification and why is it the foundation of data security? Describe common classification levels and the controls that apply to each.
choices: Data classification is the process of categorizing data based on its sensitivity and criticality, so appropriate security controls can be applied proportionally. It's the foundation of data security because you can't protect what you don't know you have, and over-protecting all data is expensive while under-protecting sensitive data is risky. Common levels: (1) Public — already approved for public release (marketing materials, public docs). Controls: minimal, integrity-focused. (2) Internal — for internal use, not sensitive if leaked (memos, project plans). Controls: access control, basic encryption. (3) Confidential — could harm the organization if leaked (financial data, customer info, proprietary code). Controls: strict access control, encryption at rest/transit, DLP, audit logging. (4) Restricted/Secret — severe harm if leaked (PII, PHI, credentials, trade secrets). Controls: encryption, MFA, least privilege, need-to-know, DLP, monitoring, legal/compliance requirements (GDPR, HIPAA). Classification drives: encryption requirements, access controls, retention policies, backup strategies, and incident response priority.

cards.question_text: Explain the difference between encryption at rest and encryption in transit. What protocols and technologies are used for each, and why are BOTH necessary?
choices: Encryption at rest protects data stored on disk/storage from unauthorized access if the storage media is compromised (stolen laptop, physical disk theft, cloud storage breach). Technologies: AES-256 (full-disk encryption like BitLocker, FileVault), database encryption (TDE — Transparent Data Encryption), cloud storage encryption (S3 SSE, Azure Storage encryption), file-level encryption (VeraCrypt). Encryption in transit protects data as it moves across networks from interception/eavesdropping (man-in-the-middle attacks, packet sniffing). Technologies: TLS/SSL (HTTPS, SMTPS, IMAPS), VPN (IPsec, WireGuard), SSH for remote access, mTLS for service-to-service. Both are necessary because they protect against different threats: encryption at rest protects against physical/disk-level access; encryption in transit protects against network-level interception. Without both: encrypting at rest but not in transit = data is readable while being transmitted; encrypting in transit but not at rest = data is readable if the disk is stolen. Defense-in-depth requires both layers.

cards.question_text: Your company stores customer PII (names, addresses, SSN, credit card numbers) in a database. A developer requests access to a copy of the production database for testing. How should you handle this request while protecting data security and complying with privacy regulations?
choices: Use data masking/tokenization to create a sanitized copy of the database for testing: (1) Replace real PII with fake but format-preserving data (e.g., real SSN 123-45-6789 becomes 456-78-9012) — this is data masking. (2) For fields that must maintain referential integrity (like customer IDs), use tokenization — replace the real value with a token that maps back to the real value via a tokenization vault, but the test environment only has tokens. (3) Alternatively, use synthetic data generation — create entirely fake datasets that match the schema and statistical properties of production data. (4) If real data is absolutely required (rare), use a secured, audited, time-limited access with DLP monitoring and a documented business justification approved by data owner + security team. (5) Never copy raw production PII to test environments — this violates GDPR (data minimization), PCI DSS (scope reduction), and internal security policies. The test DB should be out of PCI scope entirely.
Give the developer full access to the production database — they need real data for accurate testing, and developers are trusted employees

Copy the production database as-is to the test environment but tell the developer not to look at the PII fields — trust them

cards.question_text: Your DLP (Data Loss Prevention) system alerts that an employee has attempted to email a spreadsheet containing customer credit card numbers to their personal Gmail account. Upon investigation, you find the employee has done this 3 times in the past month. What is your response, and what DLP controls should be strengthened?
choices: Immediate response: (1) BLOCK the email in transit (DLP should be in blocking mode for credit card data, not just alerting). (2) QUARANTINE the spreadsheet and preserve it as evidence. (3) DISABLE the employee's email forwarding and external sending capability temporarily. (4) NOTIFY HR, the employee's manager, and the security team — this is a potential data exfiltration incident, not just a policy violation. (5) INVESTIGATE — review the employee's activity: file access logs, USB usage, cloud storage uploads, print logs. Check if data has already left the organization. (6) CONDUCT an HR/security interview — determine intent (malicious exfiltration vs. convenience/work-from-home). (7) INCIDENT RESPONSE — if malicious, follow IR procedures: preserve evidence, involve legal, consider law enforcement. If accidental (working from home), provide training and warnings. DLP STRENGTHENING: (1) Move DLP from monitor-only to block-mode for Restricted data (credit cards, SSN, PII). (2) Add content inspection rules for credit card numbers (Luhn algorithm validation, not just regex). (3) Block external email forwarding to personal domains. (4) Implement USB/portable device controls (block or encrypt-only). (5) Monitor cloud storage uploads (Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive personal). (6) Deploy endpoint DLP agents to monitor clipboard, screenshots, and file copies. (7) Implement data watermarking/fingerprinting to track exfiltrated documents.

cards.question_text: You are the CISO of a healthcare technology company that processes patient health records (PHI), payment data (PCI), and proprietary research data. Design a comprehensive data security program covering: data classification, encryption strategy, access controls, DLP, data lifecycle management, and regulatory compliance (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). How do you handle data flowing between these three regulatory regimes?
choices: COMPREHENSIVE DATA SECURITY PROGRAM: DATA CLASSIFICATION: (1) Public — marketing, published research. (2) Internal — business ops, non-PHI admin data. (3) Confidential — proprietary research, business strategy. (4) Restricted — PHI (HIPAA), cardholder data (PCI), PII (GDPR). Each data type tagged with regulatory flag (HIPAA/PCI/GDPR) for compliance routing. ENCRYPTION STRATEGY: (1) At rest: AES-256 for all Restricted data — database TDE, full-disk encryption, S3 SSE-KMS. (2) In transit: TLS 1.3 everywhere, mTLS for service-to-service. (3) Key management: AWS KMS with customer-managed keys (CMKs), separate keys per data type (PHI key, PCI key, research key), annual rotation, HSM-backed. (4) Tokenization for cardholder data — replace PAN with tokens, reducing PCI scope. (5) Field-level encryption for SSN, diagnosis codes — encrypted before hitting the database. ACCESS CONTROLS: (1) RBAC + ABAC — role defines baseline access, attributes (department, project, location) refine it. (2) Least privilege — default deny, access granted via ticket with approval. (3) Need-to-know for PHI — access only to records of patients under care. (4) MFA everywhere — FIDO2 for admins, push MFA for standard users. (5) Just-in-time (JIT) access — temporary elevated access with time limit + approval + audit. (6) Quarterly access reviews — managers certify/sub-certify their team's access. DLP: (1) Network DLP — inspect email, web uploads for PHI/PII/card data. (2) Endpoint DLP — monitor USB, clipboard, screenshots, printing. (3) Cloud DLP — CASB for SaaS apps, monitor data in Google Workspace/M365. (4) Block mode for Restricted data exiting the organization. (5) Data watermarking/fingerprinting for tracking. DATA LIFECYCLE: (1) Creation — classify and tag at creation. (2) Storage — encrypt, access-control, monitor. (3) Use — DLP in-use monitoring, need-to-know enforcement. (4) Sharing — secure file transfer, BAA with business associates (HIPAA), DLP inspection. (5) Archival — encrypted, access-restricted, indexed for retrieval. (6) Destruction — crypto-shred (destroy encryption keys), physical destruction of media, certificate of destruction. Retention: HIPAA — 6 years, PCI — 1 year (90 days for logs), GDPR — data minimization (delete when purpose fulfilled). REGULATORY COMPLIANCE: HIPAA: BAA with all business associates, audit logging of all PHI access, breach notification within 60 days. PCI DSS: tokenize card data to reduce scope, segment PCI network, quarterly ASV scans, annual SAQ/ROC. GDPR: data mapping/Inventory, DPO appointment, DPIA for high-risk processing, right to erasure process, cross-border transfer safeguards (SCCs). OVERLAPPING REGIMES: When data touches multiple regulations (e.g., patient paying by card = PHI + PCI), apply the STRICTEST controls. Map each data element to ALL applicable regulations. Data minimization — don't collect data you don't need (simplifies compliance). Segregation — keep PHI, PCI, and research data in separate databases with separate keys and access controls. Regular compliance audits — internal quarterly, external annually. Gaps analysis against each framework.
